title: Colors
summary: CSS colors can be written in names, hexadecimal, RGB, or HSL forms.

subtopics.title: Named colors
subtopics.explanation: Named colors use familiar words such as `tomato` or `navy`. They are quick to read, but the available names are limited and may not match a design palette exactly. It is like choosing from a small box of labeled crayons. Use them for simple examples; design systems usually need more controlled values. For example, choose a text and background pair, then test its contrast ratio.

subtopics.title: Hex colors
subtopics.explanation: Hexadecimal colors write red, green, and blue channels with digits, such as `#336699`. Short forms are available when each channel repeats. It is like a compact paint code on a label. Hex values are common in design tokens, but they are less intuitive to adjust by eye than some other color models. For example, use a palette token so a theme change updates related components together.

subtopics.title: RGB
subtopics.explanation: RGB describes how much red, green, and blue light combine to form a color. CSS accepts numeric channels and can include transparency. It is like mixing colored light on a screen. RGB is useful when a tool supplies channel values, but avoid changing one channel at random without checking the result in context. For example, hSL can create lighter variants by adjusting lightness while keeping a hue.

subtopics.title: HSL
subtopics.explanation: HSL describes a color by hue, saturation, and lightness. Hue is the color family; saturation is its vividness; lightness is how bright or dark it is. It is like choosing a point on a color wheel and then adjusting vividness and brightness. HSL can make related palette variations easier to reason about. For example, a transparent RGB color blends with whatever background sits beneath it.

subtopics.title: Contrast
subtopics.explanation: Contrast is the difference between foreground and background colors. Enough contrast helps people read text and identify controls. It is like using a dark marker on light paper instead of pale ink on a pale page. Check contrast for normal text, large text, focus outlines, and disabled states; color alone should not carry meaning. For example, never use color as the only signal for success, warning, or error.

foundations.overview: CSS colors change text, backgrounds, borders, and other visual details. A color can be written as a name, a hexadecimal value, or a numeric model such as RGB or HSL. Think of these formats as different ways to describe the same paint sample. Choose colors for meaning and readability, then check contrast so text remains clear for people with different vision and screens.
foundations.whyItMatters: Color affects readability and conveys state as well as appearance. A consistent palette and contrast checks make interfaces clearer across themes and visual conditions.
foundations.browserPerspective: The browser parses each color notation into an internal RGBA value (or wider-gamut representation for modern functions) and composites it with whatever is behind it, applying alpha during the paint stage.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Brand colors as hex/hsl tokens, translucent overlays with rgba, icon colors via currentColor, and contrast-checked text/background pairs are standard in every production UI.
foundations.businessImpact: Consistent, accessible color builds brand recognition and trust and widens the audience (including low-vision and colorblind users), directly affecting reach and conversion.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Defining colors as tokens (often hsl for easy tints/shades) and using currentColor reduces duplication and makes theming and dark mode far easier to implement.
foundations.performanceImpact: Color values are cheap, but heavy use of large translucent layers and many overlapping alpha-composited elements can add paint/compositing cost on low-end devices.
commonUseCases: Defining brand colors as hex or hsl tokens
Translucent overlays and shadows with rgba/alpha
Matching icon/border color to text with currentColor
Ensuring text/background pairs meet WCAG contrast

commonMisconceptions.myth: opacity and rgba alpha do the same thing.
commonMisconceptions.reality: rgba alpha makes only that color translucent; opacity fades the entire element and all its children, including text.
color sets the text (foreground/SVG) color; background-color sets the background — they are separate properties.

commonMisconceptions.myth: If it looks readable to me, the contrast is fine.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Readability varies by vision; meet measured WCAG ratios (4.5:1 for normal text) and never rely on color alone to convey meaning.

commonMisconceptions.myth: A bright color always has strong contrast against white.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Brightness alone does not determine readable contrast; test the actual foreground and background pair.

commonMisconceptions.myth: A red or green state is understandable to everyone.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Color-vision differences and assistive contexts require labels, icons, or text in addition to color.

visualExplorer.title: Ways to write the same color
visualExplorer.caption: Step through named, hex, rgb, and hsl notations that all produce the same blue, plus how alpha changes it.

steps.title: Named
steps.description: Keywords like 'royalblue' or 'tomato' are readable but limited to ~140 predefined colors.

steps.title: Hex
steps.description: #3b82f6 encodes red/green/blue as pairs of hex digits; #fff is white shorthand.

steps.title: rgb()
steps.description: rgb(59, 130, 246) sets the same color via 0-255 channels; intuitive when thinking in light channels.

steps.title: hsl()
steps.description: hsl(217, 91%, 60%) picks a hue on the wheel, then saturation and lightness — easy to make tints/shades.

steps.title: Alpha
steps.description: Adding alpha (rgba(59,130,246,0.5) or #3b82f680) makes the color translucent without affecting text on top.

interactiveExamples.title: Same color, four ways
interactiveExamples.explanation: Named, hex, rgb, and hsl can all produce the same color; pick the notation that fits your workflow.

files.index.html:
named
hex
rgb
hsl

interactiveExamples.expectedOutput: Four swatches that all render the same royal blue, demonstrating equivalent notations.

interactiveExamples.title: Alpha vs opacity
interactiveExamples.explanation: The left card uses an rgba background so its white text stays crisp; the right card uses opacity, which fades the text too.

files.index.html:
rgba background
opacity: 0.5

interactiveExamples.expectedOutput: The rgba card has a translucent dark background with fully white, readable text; the opacity card has faded text along with its background, showing the colorful gradient through everything.

codeLab.title: Build an accessible alert with currentColor
codeLab.instructions: Style .alert so its border and icon color automatically match the text color via currentColor, with a translucent background using rgba and high-contrast text. Set color once and let the border inherit it. Hints below.
codeLab.expectedOutput: A red-toned alert whose border and dot match the text color, on a subtle translucent red background, with readable text.
hints: Set color once on .alert; currentColor on the border and the dot's background will follow it.
Use rgba for a subtle translucent background so the text stays high-contrast.

keyTakeaways: Named colors use familiar words such as `tomato` or `navy`.
Hexadecimal colors write red, green, and blue channels with digits, such as `#336699`.
RGB describes how much red, green, and blue light combine to form a color.
HSL describes a color by hue, saturation, and lightness.
Contrast is the difference between foreground and background colors.
